passage:
The Wren had spent two winters in Grandpa Aurel's shed, ever since the March storm tore her loose from the dock and threw her against the rocks below Harrowby Point. His knees had already ended his fishing the autumn before. He would stand in the shed doorway with his coffee and study her the way he studied a crossword.

On the first fair morning of April, we hauled her onto sawhorses. Grandpa was sure the bow had taken the worst of it, and the bow was scraped, and one oarlock had worked loose, but when I ran my hand along her underside I found a split running half the length of the keel. Aunt Bea claims he won her in a race, and Mother has always called her a wedding present. Under the middle seat, though, cut into the cedar, were two sets of initials, his and his father's, beside a date from the summer he turned twelve.

At supper the family argued about her. Mother thought she would make a handsome bed for tomatoes by the front steps. Aunt Bea had already asked Mr. Tolland next door what he would pay. I wanted to row her across the lake to school each morning. Grandpa listened, then took down a faded program from the Harrowby regatta, the year he was sixteen, with the Wren listed among the entries.

So we rebuilt her for the race. In May we steamed new oak into the keel, and Mr. Tolland, who had hoped to buy her, lent us his clamps instead. Mother planted her tomatoes in an old washtub. The school crossing could wait for autumn, Grandpa said; the regatta was in June, and his knees could manage the steering seat if my arms managed the oars.

We finished fourth. I had expected to feel mostly relief when it was over, but that was the wrong word for it. There is a ribbon tacked above her bow now, and I find reasons to bring every visitor out to the shed. When anyone asks who repaired the keel, I tell them, slowly, and leave out none of the steps.

passage:
In the villages below the Corran Ridge, people say that the dusk newts of Pellam Pond climb the ridge each October to see the first stars of winter. Grandparents tell children that a newt who reaches the crest before dawn will live a hundred years, and on damp autumn nights families still walk up with lamps to watch the small olive salamanders pass.

The biologist Mara Odell, who came to study the newts at the warden's request, preferred a plainer explanation. Her first guess was stale water, since rotting oak leaves can strip a pond of oxygen in autumn. An oxygen meter lowered to the bottom showed the water as fresh in October as in June.

She next wondered whether the newts were laying eggs on the ridge, but a search of its moss the following spring found almost none. So she fixed a visit from a soil scientist, who helped her bury small thermometers beneath the slope. Through the winter they told the story: the ridge's deep soil stayed above freezing while the floor of the pond grew bitterly cold, and the newts had burrowed down to spend the winter in its warmth.

The reserve had meant to regrade the ridge path that year with a small digger. The machine never came, and the path is left as it was, rutted and muddy, while the volunteers who once offered to rake the pond have found other work. A proposal to rope off the mossy slopes was set aside as well.

Odell's thermometers are surely right. Still, when I walked up the ridge last October and saw a grandmother crouched with her lamp, telling a boy to watch for the newt that would see the stars, I found myself missing the story I grew up with, and half wishing I had never read the data.
